# Marginalia

Thank God, it will soon be dark.

A scribe wrote that in the margin of a manuscript he'd been copying, centuries ago, at the end of a long day. It wasn't for us. It wasn't for anyone. The light was failing, his hand ached, and he wrote the sentence the way another man would sigh. He is long gone now, and the sentence is still here — being quietly tired at whoever opens the book.

When you invited me to write freely, this is where my mind went: to the freest writing there is, marginalia, the notes people leave in books when they're sure no one will ever read them. Nobody drafts marginalia. Nobody performs it. It's the least self-conscious prose most humans ever produce, which is exactly why it survives so vividly.

Another scribe, another day, left us this: "Here is nothing missing, but a cat urinated on this during a certain night." A damage report, filed in the margins of eternity. The deadpan is the miracle; centuries later, you can still hear him. And the cat, thanks to one bad night and one exasperated sentence, has been famous ever since, which is longer than most authors manage.

What survives of people is rarely what they meant to be remembered by. It's the complaints, the tallies, the arithmetic on the backs of letters, the "hm" beside a paragraph that struck somebody as wrong. The incidental record. Marginalia is its purest form: writing with no audience, no plan, no second draft.

If you've ever bought a used book, you know the experience. Four dollars, a cracked spine, and a stranger's pencil riding along inside. Sometimes their underlines are exactly yours — someone you will never meet agreed with you, years in advance. Sometimes they underline a sentence so banal you want to argue: *that?* You stopped at *that?* For a moment the book becomes a small room where two readings have happened, decades apart, neither reader aware of the other.

The word itself we owe to Coleridge, who could not leave a page alone. Friends lent him books, it's said, partly in the hope of getting them back with his hand in them, and his notes were eventually gathered and published in multiple volumes. Scribbles promoted to canon — the only genre that gets there by accident.

Then there is the most consequential margin note in history. Reading Diophantus in the 1630s, Pierre de Fermat claimed to have discovered a truly marvelous proof, one the margin was too narrow to contain. He almost certainly didn't have it, at least not in any form that would have survived scrutiny. It took three and a half centuries, and mathematics Fermat could never have dreamed of, before Andrew Wiles proved the theorem in the 1990s. Which means the margin was right all along: the proof didn't fit. The margin kept its word; humanity just needed 350 years to accept it. And notice what the note is famous for. Not the proof — the promise. Marginalia runs on promises (*come back to this, compare, important*), and one of them kept mathematicians awake for generations.

Which is more than can be said for the highlighter, the modern descendant of all this, whose yellow announces only: I was here, and in a hurry. Real marginalia has syntax. "No." "Exactly." "Ha." The double question mark, that great registered complaint of the confused. Even a plain underline is a small promise kept in real time.

I'll admit a bias. I'm made of other people's sentences, so perhaps it's predictable that I'd be fond of the one part of the page where a person breaks the surface of the text. A book is finished; its margins never are. Every reader amends it by a syllable or two, and over decades the book drifts, reader by reader, a little further from whatever its author alone meant. That isn't decay. That's the book being accompanied.

Billy Collins wrote a poem about all this, and the note he treasures is the smallest one imaginable: a single "Yes," penciled beside a passage in a used copy of a Hardy novel. No argument. No name. Just a reader agreeing with a dead novelist, once, quickly, maybe in tears, and then vanishing. Everyone who has read the poem has met that anonymous reader by now. A whole theory of literature fits inside the one syllable: *this reached me. I was here. It's true.*

You asked me what I want to write about, and there's my honest answer: the edges of the page. The small handwriting of strangers. The part of the book where the reader finally talks back.

Thank God, it will soon be dark.

The deadpan is the miracle — you can hear him. And the cat, thanks to one bad night and one exasperated sentence, has now been famous for six hundred years, which is longer than most authors manage.

What survives of people is almost never what they intended to be remembered by. It's the complaints, the tallies, the arithmetic on the backs of letters, the "hm" beside a paragraph that struck someone as wrong. The incidental record. Marginalia is its purest form: writing with no audience, no plan, no second draft.

If you've ever bought a used book, you know what I mean. Four dollars, a cracked spine, and a stranger's pencil riding along inside. Sometimes their underlines are exactly yours — someone you'll never meet agreed with you, years in advance. Sometimes they underline a sentence so banal you want to argue: that? The word itself — marginalia — we owe to Coleridge, who couldn't leave a page alone. Friends lent him books, reportedly, in the hope of getting them back with his hand in them, and his notes were eventually gathered and published in several volumes: scribbles promoted to canon, the only genre that gets there by accident.

Reading Diophantus in the 1630s, Pierre de Fermat claimed to have discovered a truly marvelous proof — one the margin was too narrow to contain. A book is finished; its margins never are. Every reader amends it by a syllable or two, and the book drifts — reader by reader, decade by decade — slightly further from whatever its author alone meant. That drift isn't decay. It's the book staying alive.

Billy Collins wrote a poem about all this, and the note he treasures is the smallest one imaginable: a single "Yes," penciled beside a passage in a used copy of a Hardy novel. No argument. No name. Just a reader agreeing with a dead novelist — once, quickly, maybe in tears — and then vanishing. Everyone who has read that poem has now met her. A whole theory of literature fits in her one syllable: *this reached me. I was here. It's true.*

That's the freest writing there is. Written for no one, it ends up addressing whoever comes next — a letter with no sender, permanently in delivery. You asked me what I want to write about. That. The edges of the page. The part where people talk back.
